title: Willamette Valley
description: Oregon's cool valley at Burgundy's latitude, where small family wineries made Pinot Noir world-class.
L: The Willamette Valley runs about 240 km south from Portland, Oregon, between the Coast Range to the west and the Cascade Mountains to the east. It's Oregon's largest and most important wine region, with over 70% of the state's vineyards, about 11,000 hectares, and at about 45 degrees north, Burgundy's latitude.

The climate is cool and maritime: wet, mild winters and warm, dry summers, with long, cool autumns. The Coast Range blocks much Pacific rain and cold air, but the Van Duzer Corridor, a gap in the range, lets cool ocean winds in each afternoon, preserving acidity. Autumn rain at harvest is a risk.

A gap that lets cool ocean wind into the valley
It cools vineyards in the afternoon.

In 1965, David Lett planted Pinot Noir in the Dundee Hills, believing the cool climate suited it; others told him it was too cold and wet. His Eyrie Vineyards 1975 Pinot Noir placed highly in a 1979 Paris tasting against Burgundy. In 1987, Burgundy's Maison Joseph Drouhin bought land in the Dundee Hills, a vote of confidence.
The Willamette Valley lies at about the same latitude as Burgundy.
The Willamette Valley is Oregon's main region, at Burgundy's latitude

Pinot Noir is about two-thirds of the Willamette Valley's vineyards. It gives bright red cherry, raspberry, cranberry and earthy, forest floor notes, with fresh acidity and silky tannins. It's often described as between Burgundy and California in style: riper than Burgundy, fresher than California.

Pinot Gris, planted by David Lett in 1966, became Oregon's signature white: richer than Italian Pinot Grigio, with pear and spice. Chardonnay, once a struggle, is now excellent, using Dijon clones. Oregon requires 90% of a named grape on the label, stricter than the US federal 75%, for most varieties.
Oregon's 90% rule means a bottle labelled Pinot Noir is almost entirely Pinot Noir, unlike the 75% minimum elsewhere in the US.

The Dundee Hills AVA, created in 2005, is the Willamette Valley's historic heart, where David Lett and others first planted. The hills rise to about 300 m, facing south and east, above the valley's fog and frost. Famous producers include Eyrie, Domaine Drouhin Oregon, Domaine Serene and Archery Summit.

The Dundee Hills' soil is Jory, a deep, red, iron-rich clay loam formed from ancient volcanic basalt. It drains well and holds moderate water. Its Pinot Noir is known for red fruit, elegance and silky texture. Other AVAs have different soils: marine sediments in Yamhill-Carlton give darker fruit, and loess in Chehalem Mountains.
A red, iron-rich clay from volcanic basalt
It gives the Dundee Hills' elegant Pinot.

The Willamette Valley has 11 nested AVAs, including Eola-Amity Hills, cooled by the Van Duzer winds, Yamhill-Carlton, Ribbon Ridge, McMinnville, Chehalem Mountains and Laurelwood District. Each has distinct soils, volcanic, marine sediment or loess, giving different Pinot styles.

Reading Oregon and eating with it

Labels show the winery, grape, AVA, like Willamette Valley or Dundee Hills, and vintage. Oregon's rules are strict: 90% of a named grape, 95% from a named AVA, and no use of European place names like Burgundy. Most wineries are small and family-owned; many are certified sustainable, LIVE, or biodynamic.

Willamette Pinot Noir suits salmon, especially Pacific Northwest grilled or cedar-plank salmon, duck, mushrooms, truffles, pork and roast chicken. Pinot Gris suits seafood, Dungeness crab and Asian food. Chardonnay suits halibut and creamy dishes. Serve Pinot at 14 to 16 degrees.
